fr:title.text: Sketches of an elephant: a topos theory compendium

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sketches of an elephant: a topos theory compendium

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In this section, we give an overview of the basic setup for the type theory: a category with families (CwF).
In The Elephant, Johnstone makes the following definitions for “theory”; we will call this an elephant theory in order to distinguish it from other notions of theory we might consider.

For \mathcal {S} a topos, an elephant theory over \mathcal {S} is a (pseudo-)functor T \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat}, where (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} is the 2-category of bounded geometric morphisms into \mathcal {S} and \mathsf {Cat} is the 2-category of large categories.
A morphism of elephant theories is simply an indexed functor.

We say that T is classified by \mathsf {S}[T] \colon \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S} if T is contravariantly represented by \mathcal {S}[T], that is T(\mathcal {E}) \cong \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}(\mathcal {E}, \mathcal {S}[T]). We also call \mathsf {S}[T] the classifying topos for T.
(See Elephant Definition B4.2.1)

The object classifier \mathbb {O} is the elephant theory defined by the forgetful functor (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} which sends a bounded topos over \mathcal {S} to its underlying category of objects.
(See Elephant Example B4.2.4(a))
If T is a geometric theory, then a geometric construct is a \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}-indexed functor F \colon T \to \mathbb {O}.
The idea is that F, given a model M of T in an \mathcal {S}-topos \mathcal {E}, produces an object of \mathcal {E}.
(See Elephant Definition B4.2.5)
Geometric theories may be consicely defined as the elephant theories built up via a sequence of product-inserter-equifier limits starting from the object classifier.
We expand this to give more intuition.

If T is a theory, a simple functional extension of T is another theory T' given as the inserter of two geometric constructs F,G \colon T \to \mathbb {O}. Intuitively, T' is the theory given by freely adding a new morphism between the “objects” F and G.

If T is a theory, a simple equational extension of T is another theory T' given as the equifier of two indexed natural transformations \alpha , \beta \colon F \Rightarrow G, where F and G are geometric constructs. Intuitively, T' is the theory given by adding a new equality between morphisms of “objects”.
A geometric theory is a theory built up by a finite sequence T_0,\ldots ,T_n of simple functional extensions and simple equational extensions starting from T_0 = \mathbb {O}^m for some finite m.

(See Elephant Definition 4.2.7, note that Johnstone gives a slightly different definition, using simple geometric quotients in place of simple equational extensions, which use inverters instead of equifiers. The name “simple equational extension” is not known to us to be previously used, but it follows the schema of “simple functional extension.”)
Any geometric theory has a classifying topos.
(See Elephant Theorem 4.2.9)

fr:title.text: A category with families structure on elephant theories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A category with families structure on elephant theories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let \mathsf {ElTh} be the category of elephant theories. Then let \mathsf {Ty} \colon \mathsf {ElTh}^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {SET} be the large presheaf which sends an elephant theory \Gamma to the set of strict 2-functors A \colon (\int \Gamma )^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat}.

Intuitively, \mathsf {Ty}(\Gamma ) is “elephant theories relative to \Gamma .” This is because \int \Gamma is the category of topoi equipped with a model of \Gamma ; if \Gamma were a geometric theory then \int \Gamma would be equivalent to \mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S}[\Gamma ].

Then define \mathsf {Tm} \colon (\int \mathsf {Ty})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Set} by letting \mathsf {Tm}(\Gamma , A) be the set of sections of A. A section a is a natural assignment of a(\mathcal {E}, M) \colon A(\mathcal {E}, M) for (\mathcal {E},M) \in \int \Gamma .

Context extension is given in the following way. Suppose that \Gamma \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} is a context and A \colon \mathsf {Ty}(\Gamma ). Then \Gamma \triangleright A \colon (\mathsf {BTop}/\mathcal {S})^\mathrm {op} \to \mathsf {Cat} is defined by (\Gamma \triangleright A)(\mathcal {E}) = (M \colon \Gamma (\mathcal {E})) \times A(\mathcal {E},M).
Then finally we have weakening and the variable rule given by the first and second projections out of \Gamma \triangleright A.
Note that even though topoi and elephant theories are non-trivially 2-categorical, (\mathsf {ElTh},\mathsf {Ty},\mathsf {Tm}) forms nevertheless a strict (albeit quite large) category with families.
